### Supporting basis

Zstandard at level 3 significantly outperforms gzip at level 6 in both speed and ratio. While gzip level 6 offers a reasonable balance, it is computationally heavier for the compression gained. Zstandard’s dictionary-based compression excels with structured data like newline-delimited JSON. Repeated field names, timestamps, and identifiers create high redundancy. Zstandard’s default 256 KB dictionary window captures these patterns efficiently across the 10 GB dataset. For logs with 1 KB records, the overhead of managing small streams is negligible with Zstandard’s optimized single-thread implementation. Gzip’s LZ77 algorithm struggles with longer-term redundancies in large archives compared to Zstandard’s FSE and Huffman coding. Consequently, Zstandard achieves a better size-to-speed ratio, crucial when writing once and decompressing repeatedly. This reduces I/O wait times significantly during frequent reads, leveraging memory bandwidth more effectively than gzip.

### Recommendation

For your specific workload, Zstandard at compression level 3 is the superior choice. Empirical benchmarks on similar log datasets show Zstandard level 3 compresses ~2-3% smaller than gzip level 6 while being 3-5x faster in compression. Decompression is 2-4x faster with Zstandard, which is critical for your repeated read pattern. Decompression speed directly impacts application latency during log analysis or replay. The slightly larger binary dependency is outweighed by reduced CPU load and storage costs. Gzip is ubiquitous but suboptimal for high-throughput, repeated-decompression scenarios. Zstandard provides a better total cost of ownership by lowering cloud egress costs (smaller size) and improving query performance (faster decompression). Given the newline-delimited structure and repeated JSON keys, Zstandard’s dictionary mode will exploit these patterns effectively, making it the most practical and performant option for modern infrastructure.<|im_end|>
